cues.text: A Relic Amid Legend
In a small chapel off the great Gothic nave of Valencia Cathedral sits a modest cup of dark red agate, barely nine centimeters tall.
It is mounted on a base of gold, pearls, and gemstones added centuries after the cup itself was carved.
Pilgrims and skeptics alike have called it the most credible surviving candidate for the Holy Grail, the very vessel Christ raised at the Last Supper.
Two popes have said Mass with it in their hands.
What the cup cannot offer is certainty, and honesty about that uncertainty is itself part of the story it has to tell.

Archaeologists who have examined the upper cup agree it is a genuine ancient vessel, an Eastern Mediterranean piece carved from banded agate sometime between the first century before Christ and the first century after.
That much is established fact.

Whether this particular cup passed through the hands of Christ and the apostles in an upper room in Jerusalem is a claim resting entirely on tradition, carried forward by devotion long before it was carried forward by documents.
From Jerusalem to Rome

Catholic tradition holds that the cup remained at Rome, used by the early popes, until the persecution of Emperor Valerian in the mid-third century, when Pope St. Sixtus II entrusted it to his deacon, St. Lawrence, for safekeeping.
Lawrence, a native of the region near Huesca in Spain, is said to have sent the relic to his homeland shortly before his own martyrdom in 258.

This account belongs to long-standing tradition rather than early documentary testimony, and it should be received as such: a venerable memory the Church has cherished, not a record a modern historian could trace and confirm step by step.
Hidden Through Centuries of Conquest
Documented history begins centuries later.
During the Muslim conquest of Spain after 713, the relic was moved through a succession of Pyrenean refuges.
It finally came to rest at the monastery of San Juan de la Peña in the mountains of Aragon, where a document from 1071 explicitly records a precious stone chalice among the monastery's treasures.
There it remained under Benedictine care for more than three hundred years, a treasured but largely private possession of the mountain community that guarded it.
Into the Treasury of Aragon
The chalice entered public history in 1399, when the monks surrendered it to King Martin of Aragon in exchange for royal favor, and it passed into the treasury of the Crown of Aragon.
His successor, King Alfonso the Magnanimous, brought it to the royal palace in Valencia around 1424.
In 1437, with Alfonso occupied in Naples, the relic was given over with the rest of the royal reliquary to Valencia Cathedral.
It has remained there ever since, apart from two wartime exiles: once to Mallorca during the Napoleonic invasion and once to the town of Carlet during the Spanish Civil War.
Veneration Today

Since 1916 the cup has been kept in its own chapel within the cathedral, brought out for veneration each Holy Thursday and on a feast day in late October, when it is carried in procession to the high altar.
In the modern era, it has drawn the attention of two popes.
St. John Paul II celebrated Mass with the Santo Cáliz during his 1982 visit to Valencia, and Benedict XVI did the same in 2006.
Each treated the relic not as a settled archaeological verdict, but as an object worthy of reverence within a living tradition of faith.
What draws pilgrims to this small cup, finally, is not proof but continuity: the sense of an unbroken thread of devotion.

That thread stretches from an upper room in Jerusalem, through the deserts of persecution and the mountains of a besieged Christian kingdom, to a cathedral chapel where the faithful still kneel before it today.
Whether or not this is the very cup Christ held, it stands as a sign of something the Church has always believed, regardless of any single relic.
The gift given at the Last Supper did not end that night, but has been carried forward, cup after cup, to every altar where the Eucharist is still offered.
